title: graph models, representations, and traversal
concepts: A graph consists of vertices and edges; edges may be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, and the problem statement determines which model applies.
An adjacency list stores each vertex's neighbors and uses O(V+E) space; an adjacency matrix uses O(V²) space and supports constant-time edge lookup.
Depth-first search explores a path before backtracking and can be implemented recursively or with an explicit stack; breadth-first search explores by distance layers using a queue.
In an unweighted graph, BFS discovers shortest paths by edge count; DFS does not generally provide shortest paths.
A visited set prevents repeated work and infinite loops in cyclic graphs; mark timing affects whether duplicate work can enter a traversal frontier.
Starting a traversal from every still-unvisited vertex labels connected components in an undirected graph; directed reachability requires different notions such as strongly connected components.
Bipartite testing colors neighbors with opposite colors and detects a conflict when an edge joins same-colored vertices.
A grid can be modeled as an implicit graph whose edges are valid neighbor moves, avoiding explicit storage of every adjacency list.
